title: Using Multiple-Origin Composition in SAP OData Provisioning for BAS Development
author: Srivatsa
text:
Introduction 
 While migrating SAP Fiori applications from SAP Web IDE to SAP Business Application Studio, we investigated Multiple-Origin Composition (MOC) in SAP OData Provisioning as an alternative way of accessing backend data during local development. 
 MOC is designed for an OData service that is assigned to multiple backend destinations. Instead of accessing only the default backend, OData Provisioning can retrieve data from multiple origins and compose the successful results into one service response. MOC also supports OData $batch requests. Multi Origin Composition [https://he...6bfca.html] 
 In our scenario, the default backend destination used Principal Propagation and had to remain the default because productive SAP Build Work Zone users depended on it. During our initial BAS testing, the required business-user context was not available through the authentication method being tested, while a second destination using technical authentication could successfully access the same backend service. 
 Changing the ODP default destination was not acceptable because it would also affect productive users. Creating another Integration Suite landscape purely for development was also unnecessary. MOC therefore provided a useful temporary option for local BAS development. 
 It worked particularly well for collection-oriented scenarios such as tables, searches and value helps. However, it also exposed an important limitation: MOC makes the OData service origin-aware. Existing applications that assume a normal single-origin entity key may therefore require application changes for single-entity navigation and update scenarios. 
 What Multiple-Origin Composition Does 
 Normally, a registered OData service called without MOC uses its configured default destination. 
 With MOC, OData Provisioning can access multiple destinations assigned to the service and compose their results. 
 SAP documents the MOC read URL using the service version followed by ;mo : Multi Origin Composition [https://he...6bfca.html] 
 /odata/<namespace>/<service>;<version>;mo/<EntitySet> 
 For $batch , the corresponding URL is: 
 /odata/<namespace>/<service>;<version>;mo/$batch 
 If ;mo is omitted, OData Provisioning uses only the default system. Multi Origin Composition [https://he...6bfca.html] 
 MOC is therefore more than simple URL routing. It changes how OData Provisioning resolves the registered service and how entities from different origins are represented. 
 Our BAS Development Scenario 
 Our registered OData service had two backend destinations. 
 The first destination used Principal Propagation and remained the productive default. 
 The second destination used technical authentication and could access the same backend service without depending on the interactive business-user context. 
 During our initial BAS testing, the default Principal Propagation destination could not complete the request successfully, while the technical origin could. 
 We wanted to preserve the productive ODP configuration, so instead of changing the default destination, we used MOC only during local BAS development. 
 Using MOC Only During Local BAS Development 
 We did not put ;mo into the productive manifest.json . 
 Instead, we used a separate ui5-local.yaml and the SAP Fiori Tools fiori-tools-proxy middleware to rewrite the service path during local preview. 
 The application continued using its normal /backend OData URL. 
 For metadata, we kept the regular ODP service URL. For collection and $batch traffic, the local proxy changed the service root to its MOC form. 
 For example, a local request to: 
 /backend/odata/sap/Z_SAMPLE_SERVICE_SRV/ 
 was routed to: 
 /odata/sap/Z_SAMPLE_SERVICE_SRV;v=1;mo/ 
 while metadata continued to use: 
 /odata/sap/Z_SAMPLE_SERVICE_SRV/$metadata 
 This allowed the SAPUI5 application itself to remain unaware of the local MOC configuration. 
 The important point was that the change existed only in ui5-local.yaml . The application deployed to SAP Build Work Zone remained on the normal OData contract. 
 Error Tolerance Was Essential 
 MOC alone was not sufficient in our scenario. 
 By default, when one of the destinations participating in MOC returns an error, that failure can cause the composed request to fail. 
 SAP OData Provisioning provides Error Tolerance for this situation. When Error Tolerance is enabled, an error is returned only when data retrieval from all participating backends fails. If only some origins fail, successfully retrieved data from the remaining origins can still be returned. Multi Origin Composition [https://he...6bfca.html] 
 In our test, the Principal Propagation origin failed while the technical origin succeeded. 
 After enabling Error Tolerance , OData Provisioning could return the data from the successful origin rather than failing the entire BAS request. 
 Without Error Tolerance, MOC did not solve our local scenario because the inaccessible origin could still cause the complete request to fail. 
 Metadata Caching Was Equally Important 
 We also found that Error Tolerance alone was not enough . 
 The stable configuration in our environment required Metadata Cache to be enabled and Destination-Based Metadata Caching to be disabled . 
 This mattered because one participating destination could not be accessed successfully by the current BAS caller. 
 Disabling destination-based metadata caching allowed OData Provisioning to work with common cached metadata instead of tying metadata processing to the inaccessible origin. 
 This configuration should only be used when the participating destinations expose compatible metadata for the registered service. 
 After changing the cache configuration, we cleared the existing service metadata cache so OData Provisioning could rebuild it using the new settings. 
 The Combination That Worked 
 No single setting solved the BAS scenario by itself. 
 The combination that worked for us was MOC in the local runtime URL, Error Tolerance enabled, Metadata Cache enabled, Destination-Based Metadata Caching disabled, and at least one backend origin capable of returning data successfully . 
 This allowed BAS to consume real backend data without changing the productive default destination. 
 Where MOC Worked Well 
 MOC worked particularly well for collection-oriented operations. 
 We successfully used it for list and table data, value helps, search results, filtering, collection reads, OData $batch requests and initial application loading . 
 These scenarios fit MOC naturally because they primarily process feeds or collections that can be composed from several origins. 
 For a list-oriented application, this can support a significant part of local development. 
 The Important Limitation: SAP__Origin 
 The main application-level limitation appeared when we tested single-entity navigation. 
 Consider a normal OData service where an entity is identified by one business key: 
 BusinessEntity('1000123') 
 In a single-origin service, that is sufficient because 1000123 uniquely identifies the entity. 
 With MOC, the same business key can potentially exist in more than one backend origin. 
 For example, 1000123 could exist in both ORIGIN_A and ORIGIN_B . 
 The business key by itself is therefore no longer enough to identify which physical backend record is intended. 
 The MOC representation introduces origin information, commonly exposed using SAP__Origin , so the entity can remain associated with its actual backend origin. 
 Conceptually, a normal entity identity such as: 
 BusinessEntity('1000123') 
 can become an origin-aware identity similar to: 
 BusinessEntity(BusinessKey='1000123',SAP__Origin='ORIGIN_A') 
 The exact business-key property name and the actual value of SAP__Origin must always come from the real MOC service metadata and response. They should not be guessed or hardcoded. 
 What Happened in Our Custom Application 
 Our custom SAPUI5 application was originally built for a single-origin OData service. 
 Some application logic navigated to individual records using the normal service contract. Conceptually, the resulting request looked like: 
 BusinessEntity('1000123') 
 Collection requests through MOC worked correctly. 
 However, when the application tried to address an individual entity using the original single-key representation, OData Provisioning rejected the request because the MOC version of the entity expected origin-aware key information. 
 In our case, the error indicated that the expected key predicate information was incomplete. 
 This was not a BAS connectivity failure and it was not an authentication problem. 
 The application was using the key contract of the original single-origin service against the origin-aware MOC representation. 
 A useful diagnostic pattern therefore emerged: the list page can work while object-level navigation fails . 
 When this happens with MOC, entity-key handling should be investigated before assuming that the backend connection is failing. 
 Why Custom Applications May Need Program Changes 
 If MOC is going to become part of a custom application's supported architecture, the application needs to become origin-aware . 
 An application that previously retained only a business key such as 1000123 may also have to preserve the SAP__Origin value returned with that entity. 
 When the application subsequently addresses that entity, it needs to use the complete identity expected by the MOC service. 
 This can affect single-entity reads, object-page navigation, navigation-property requests, $expand , updates, deletes, deep links, actions, function calls and entity operations inside $batch requests . 
 The application should not simply hardcode something such as SAP__Origin='ORIGIN_A' . 
 Different records can originate from different backend systems. The origin must therefore come from the actual selected entity returned by the service. 
 Prefer Metadata-Driven Entity-Key Handling 
 A custom SAPUI5 application intended to support MOC should avoid manually concatenating OData URLs wherever possible. 
 A legacy implementation may assume that an entity always has one unnamed string key and construct a path such as: 
 BusinessEntity('1000123') 
 A MOC-capable implementation may need enough information to construct an origin-aware entity identity such as: 
 BusinessEntity(BusinessKey='1000123',SAP__Origin='ORIGIN_A') 
 The exact canonical format must be determined from the actual MOC metadata. 
 The required application change is therefore not simply "append SAP__Origin to every URL." 
 Instead, the application must treat the entity as an origin-aware OData entity and retain the complete identity returned by the service. 
 Navigation Properties Are Affected Too 
 The impact is not limited to direct single-entity reads. 
 An existing application might navigate using: 
 BusinessEntity('1000123')/ToAttachments 
 or: 
 BusinessEntity('1000123')?$expand=ToAttachments 
 If MOC changes the parent entity into an origin-aware identity, the parent must first be identified correctly before OData Provisioning can resolve the related entities. 
 Conceptually, the MOC-aware request may therefore need the origin as part of the parent key before navigating to ToAttachments . 
 This is why simply adding ;mo to the service URL can be enough for the initial table to load while object-page navigation still fails later. 
 $batch Requires Additional Attention 
 MOC officially supports $batch . SAP documents the MOC batch URL as /odata/<namespace>/<service>;<version>;mo/$batch . Multi Origin Composition [https://he...6bfca.html] 
 However, the outer $batch URL is only part of the request. 
 The multipart $batch body contains individual OData requests. 
 If one of those embedded requests addresses a specific entity, that embedded request must also use the correct origin-aware entity identity. 
 An operation that previously addressed BusinessEntity('1000123') may therefore also need the appropriate SAP__Origin when executed in

title: What's New in Service Management in SAP Cloud ERP Private 2025 FPS02
author: DequanXu
text:
The SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2025 FPS2 release brings a rich set of innovations to Service Management. From AI-powered contract management powered by SAP Joule to expanded in-house service logistics, this release focuses on reducing manual effort, improving transparency, and enabling smarter, more connected service processes. Below is a detailed overview of every new feature in this release. 

 Service Contract Management 

 AI-assisted management of expiring service contracts with Joule Skill 
 This feature introduces a dedicated Joule Skill for managing expiring service contracts directly through SAP Joule, the AI copilot embedded in SAP S/4HANA. Contract managers can ask Joule in natural language to show all service contracts expiring within a user-defined time frame. From within the Joule conversation, they can then run extension scenarios such as configuring auto-renewal for a specific item, renewing an entire contract, renewing all line items at once, or renewing a single line item. Quick action buttons for these operations appear directly in the chat response, as shown in the screenshots below. 

 By combining intelligent search and guided renewal actions in a single conversational experience, contract managers can act on expiring contracts much faster than navigating through traditional menus. The feature reduces the risk of missed renewals, supports proactive contract governance, and lowers the administrative overhead for teams handling large contract portfolios. Available for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition only. 

 Joule based search and status update of service contracts with Joule Skill 
 A second Joule Skill for service contracts enables users to search for contracts by employee name or product name, and to change the lifecycle status of a contract item to 'Released' or 'Completed' — all without leaving the Joule interface. The screenshot below shows a Joule query filtering contracts for a specific employee and product, returning matching results with an option to perform lifecycle actions directly from the response. 

 This capability significantly streamlines daily contract processing tasks for contract managers. By combining targeted search and immediate status updates in one conversational interaction, it eliminates the need to switch between apps, apply complex filters, and navigate individual records. The result is reduced administrative overhead, faster turnaround on contract lifecycle decisions, and an improved day-to-day experience. Available for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition only. 

 AI-assisted enterprise search with service contracts 
 Service contracts can now be discovered using natural language queries typed directly into the SAP Fiori Launchpad search field. Users select the 'Service Contract' category from the scope selector and type a plain-language query — for example, 'Show service contracts with status Completed' — and the system returns instant, relevant results leveraging natural language processing. The screenshot below illustrates the search experience with a natural language query returning a filtered list of completed contracts. 

 This feature removes the barrier of needing to know system-specific syntax or how to configure complex filters, making contract discovery accessible to a much broader set of users. Faster results, reduced navigation steps, and a lower learning curve all contribute to improved productivity and easier adoption across the organization. Available for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition only. 

 Additional attributes for managing and mass changing service contracts 
 New search attributes have been added to both the 'Manage Service Contracts' and 'Mass Change Service Contracts' apps. Users can now filter and retrieve contracts by equipment, functional location, and product. The screenshots below show the new Equipment, Functional Location, and Product filter fields highlighted in the filter bar of both apps. 

 These additional search dimensions mean service teams can instantly pinpoint contracts tied to a specific piece of equipment or a location, without manual filtering or scrolling through large result sets. This directly supports faster responses to customer inquiries and more efficient contract administration — all delivered out of the box with no customization required. Available for both SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition and SAP S/4HANA. 

 Addition of a "Select-all", "Set/Remove Billing Block" and "Set Completed" feature in the mass-change app 
 The Mass Change Service Contracts app has been enhanced with three new capabilities. A 'Select All' checkbox allows users to automatically select all entries in the list in one click — as shown in the first screenshot where 1,653 contracts are selected simultaneously. Two additional mass change actions have also been introduced: 'Set Billing Block', 'Remove Billing Block', and 'Set to Completed', accessible from the Change dropdown menu as shown in the second screenshot. 

 Processing hundreds or thousands of service contracts individually is error-prone and time-consuming. These enhancements transform that manual process into a streamlined bulk operation, dramatically reducing processing time, minimizing the risk of accidentally skipping items, and improving overall throughput for contract administrators. Available for both SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition and SAP S/4HANA. 

 Contract management optimization through harmonized document management capabilities 
 Service contracts now support harmonized document management (HDM), leveraging the SAP Document Management service for modern, cost-effective file storage. Users can upload and manage attachments of multiple document types — including SAT Attachments and GOS Attachments — directly from the Attachments tab of the service contract, as shown in the screenshot below. The implementation is consistent with the HDM approach used across other SAP S/4HANA service applications. 

 A harmonized document management experience across service applications reduces the overhead of working with different attachment interfaces in different contexts. It simplifies integration with output management, approval workflows, and third-party document management systems, while providing a user-friendly, consistent interface for all document-related tasks. Available for both SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition and SAP S/4HANA. 

 Enabling process flow for service contracts 
 The service contract header overview page now includes a graphical Process Flow section that provides a read-only, visual representation of all connected business documents. Documents are organized into distinct lanes — Service Contract, Billing Document Request, Invoice, Cancellation Invoice, Credit Memo Request, Credit Memo, and Accounting Document — as illustrated in the screenshots below. Clicking a node in the flow reveals quick-navigation links to related apps and document details. 

 Having a clear, real-time view of the full transaction history from within the contract record greatly reduces the time needed to locate related documents and understand the current state of a billing cycle. It strengthens auditability, simplifies error investigation, and improves user confidence in the correctness of service-to-cash processes. Available for both SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition and SAP S/4HANA. 

 Multilevel categorization available as a search attribute in API and apps 
 Multilevel categorization is now available as a search and filter attribute in the Manage Service Contracts app, the Mass Change Service Contracts app, and the Service Contract OData API. The screenshot below shows the new Categorization filter field in use, filtering contracts by a specific software category value. 

 Categorization makes it easier to organize large contract portfolios, retrieve relevant records faster with advanced, hierarchical search criteria, and support better reporting and decision-making. The feature also benefits API consumers who can now include categorization filters in automated contract retrieval scenarios. Available for both SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition and SAP S/4HANA. 

 Service Quotation and Order Management 

 Order-Based Quotation 
 A new order-based quotation capability allows users to create and update service quotations directly sourced from service order items. Service products, service parts, and expenses recorded in a service order can be copied into an order-based quotation to communicate the scope and estimated costs to the customer. As service execution progresses and additional services or spare parts are added to the order, the linked quotation can be updated to reflect the revised scope and pricing. The screenshot below shows the 'Create/Update Quotation' action available from within a service order. 

 This capability establishes transparent change management throughout the service engagement lifecycle. Customers receive clear, up-to-date communication on scope and cost at every stage of the process, while service organizations benefit from a single, continuously updated service order linked to a formal quotation. This ensures cost visibility, supports formal approval workflows, and reduces disputes over scope or billing. Available for both SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition and SAP S/4HANA. 

 Condition entry in item list of service transactions 
 Users can now enter price conditions directly in the item list of service transactions — service orders and service quotations — without navigating to the individual item detail page. A new Condition Amount and Condition Type column is now visible and editable inline in the item list, as shown in the screenshot below. The configuration entry point in customizing ('Define Condition Types for Easy Condition Entry') controls which condition types are exposed in the item list. 

 Reducing the number of navigation steps required to set pricing on service items directly improves the speed and ergonomics of order entry. Service agents can process orders more efficiently, resulting in a better user experience and shorter order-creation times. Available for both SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition and SAP S/4HANA. 

 Equipment and Functional Location Objects in Service Order and Quotation Item Lists 
 The item lists of Service Orders and Service Quotations now support displaying and maintaining the main Equipment ID and Functional Location ID directly in the item list, without opening each item's detail page. As shown in the screenshot below, the new 'Equipment ID (Main Ref. Obj.)' and 'Functional Location ID (Ma...)' columns appear inline in the Items tab. 

 This enhancement significantly improves usability for service advisors and planners who need to assign or review reference objects across multiple items at once. Eliminating unnecessary navigation to item overviews saves time and reduces cognitive load, especially on complex orders with many line items. Available for both SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition and SAP S/4HANA. 

 Service organization for Inter-Company Service order process 
 In the intercompany service order process, it is now possible to record not only the Sales Organization of the service-executing company but also its Service Organization in the customer-facing service order. In addition, the execution status from the executing service company is automatically updated back into the customer-facing service order. The screenshots below show the updated service order fields for intercompany scenarios. 

 This improvement closes an important gap in intercompany service scenarios by enabling complete organizational assignment and real-time status visibility across company boundaries. It enhances service delivery efficiency, reduces errors in fulfillment, and gives all stakeholders — including the customer-facing team — a transparent view of order progress. Available for both SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition and SAP S/4HANA.

title: How AI Is Reshaping SAPUI5: From Development to Runtime to Extensibility
author: OliverGraeff
text:
TL;DR: AI has arrived across the entire SAPUI5 lifecycle. Whether you write code, adapt apps, apply themes, or just use a business application, there is an AI capability for you today. This post shows: what is available, where to find it, and how to get started. 

 Over the past two years, we have introduced AI capabilities across virtually every phase of SAPUI5 application development and beyond. What started with Joule in SAP Build Code has grown into a comprehensive set of tools, from AI-powered coding agents and MCP servers to Joule interacting with applications at runtime. 
 AI in the context of SAPUI5 touches different personas in different phases, and the best entry point depends on your role. Let us walk through what is available, organized by who benefits and when. 

 For the Developer: AI-Assisted UI5 Development 
 UI5 Plugins for Coding Agents 
 Agentic AI: MCP Server and Plugins for Coding Agents 
 Joule in SAP Build Code is one path. But many developers use external coding agents like Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, or others, as part of their daily workflow. Generic AI tools do not understand the specifics of SAPUI5: the class system, the module loader, the manifest structure, the linter rules. That is where the UI5 MCP Server and the UI5 Plugins for Coding Agents come in. 
 The UI5 Plugins for Coding Agents are an open-source collection of plugins, introduced for Claude Code , also available for GitHub Copilot . The plugin family currently includes these plugins: 
 UI5 plugin, your general development companion: project scaffolding, API documentation, linting, best-practice guidelines, UI integration cards, OPA5 integration tests and UI5 tables, wrapping the UI5 MCP server 
 UI5 TypeScript Conversion plugin, a step-by-step TypeScript migration with UI5-specific rules 
 UI5 Modernization plugin, a five-phase autonomous workflow that modernizes a legacy SAPUI5 app to current best practices: replacing deprecated APIs, eliminating global namespaces, updating the manifest, and preparing for Content Security Policy compliance. What used to take weeks can now be accomplished in hours. 
 The UI5 MCP Server is an open-source Model Context Protocol server that gives any MCP-compatible AI agent deep SAPUI5 knowledge, which is official, correct and up to date. This provides UI5-specifics that generic tools consistently get wrong. The UI5 MCP server provides tools for: 
 Creating UI5 apps by scaffolding new applications based on latest best practices, 
 Fetching necessary data like current SAPUI5 version information, latest development best practices as well as the applicable UI5 API documentation, 
 Running the UI5 linter to analyze and report issues your existing UI5 application code, 
 Migrating apps to TypeScript by guiding the agent through a correct JavaScript-to-TypeScript conversion, and 
 UI Integration Cards to scaffold and validate UI Integration Cards following official best practices. 
 The key design principle here is that these tools are agent-agnostic. The same SAPUI5 knowledge is available regardless of which coding agent you prefer. And they are open source: contributions welcome. 
 Agentic SAPUI5 development in SAP Build Code 
 Joule in SAP Build Code offers agentic development in SAP Business Application Studio (BAS) via the AI Chat , which leverages a configured provider (such as SAP AI Core, a third-party LLM provider, or GitHub Copilot). This uses the UI5 MCP Server to bring the mentioned UI5 qualities into your development flow. 
 Developing Apps with UI5 Web Components 
 The AI tooling story extends to UI5 Web Components as well. The UI5 Web Components MCP Server gives AI coding agents direct access to component APIs, framework integration guides for React, Angular, and vanilla JavaScript, and the full documentation corpus. Complementing the MCP server, three installable Agent Skills provide domain-specific best practices for styling, accessibility, and visual testing. Together, they ensure your AI assistant generates accurate UI5 Web Components code regardless of the framework you use. 
 Summarizing: 

 Entry Point 
 What It Does 
 Link 

 UI5 Plugins for Coding Agents 
 Plugins for Claude Code and GitHub Copilot for UI5 development, modernization, TypeScript conversion github.com/UI5/plugins-coding-agents 

 UI5 MCP Server 
 MCP tools for any AI agent: TypeScript migration, Integration Cards, best practices 
 github.com/UI5/mcp-server 

 SAP Build Code -> AI Chat 
 Agentic SAPUI5 development within SAP Build Code 
 SAP Build Code: AI chat 

 UI5 Web Components MCP Server and Skills 
 Component APIs, framework guides, Styling, accessibility, and visual testing best practices for apps using UI5 Web Components. 
 UI5 Web Components MCP Server 

 Skills documentation 

 At Runtime: AI Meets the Running Application 
 Joule in UI Theme Designer 
 AI does not stop at the IDE. Several capabilities bring intelligence to the running application itself, whether it is an SAP Fiori app, an SAP GUI transaction, or via the UI theme designer. 
 Joule Frontend Actions 
 With Frontend Actions , Joule can interact directly with the application UI running in the user's browser or desktop client. Joule can execute scripted interactions, guide users step by step through a process, or read and summarize the current screen. This works across UI technologies, in SAPUI5, SAP GUI for HTML, and Web Dynpro. 
 The pattern is the same: an application exposes actions to Joule, and Joule orchestrates them in response to the user's natural-language request. A user might type "create a new product" and Joule navigates the transaction, fills fields, switches tabs, and confirms dialogs on the user's behalf. 
 SAPUI5 provides a unified API for registering custom actions with SAP Joule (planned feature). Generic actions (such as describeUI, describeUIElement, setFields, executeAction) are registered automatically. See the details in Joule Frontend Actions – Let SAP's AI Assistant Talk to Your Application UI in SAPUI5 and Beyond . 
 AI-Ready UI5 Web Components for Your Apps 
 If you are building AI capabilities into your own applications, the @ui5/webcomponents-ai package provides dedicated UI building blocks for AI interaction workflows. One example is the AI Prompt Input giving users a natural-language entry field with a submit action. Accompanying these components, the AI Patterns catalog defines interaction blueprints, from first-use acknowledgement dialogs and quick-prompt templates to guided prompts and regeneration loops, so you do not have to design the AI UX from scratch. 
 Theming with AI Support 
 Theming is a critical but often underestimated part of customizing enterprise apps. Two new capabilities bring AI to this space: 
 The UI Theme Designer plugin for coding agents gives AI assistants grounded knowledge of the SAP design system: design tokens, theme parameters, and how they map to SAPUI5 controls, SAP Build Work Zone, and SAP S/4HANA. Install it with a single command and your coding agent handles theming tasks with the precision of a theming expert. 
 Complementing this, Joule is now available directly inside the UI Theme Designer on SAP BTP. You can ask questions about custom theme creation, tool usage, and design concepts in natural language, without leaving the tool. Joule draws on the official documentation to deliver summarized answers and links to relevant help content. 
 Joule Work and the UI Foundation 
 Looking ahead, Joule Work represents a shift in how SAP redefines user experiences. Rather than building every UI as a separately coded screen, Joule Work is built on the Compositional Design System : A model where AI can compose user experiences at runtime using reusable components and shared design knowledge. 
 No matter what UI technology, proven enterprise-grade qualities are a must for solutions in an SAP context. This is still evolving, but the direction is clear: a consistent, scalable development foundation which follows AI-native UX concepts. 

 For Extensibility: AI-Supported Adaptation 
 Joule in SAPUI5 Adaptation Editor 
 SAPUI5 flexibility allows key users and developers to extend standard SAP Fiori applications in an upgrade-safe way, without modifying the original source code. Today, key users can rearrange, hide, or rename fields directly in the running app. Developers can go further in adaptation projects, extending the UI with custom code. We are planning to let Joule support both personas in their adaptation workflows: 
 For key users , the vision is to let your business describe desired UI changes in natural language ("move the delivery date field next to the order number" or "hide the internal reference section") and let Joule translate that into the necessary changes in the system. This lowers the barrier to entry for users who are not familiar with the drag-and-drop adaptation mode and makes adaptations more discoverable. 
 Developers come into the game if these changes require custom code: Joule decides that an adaptation project is required and supports the next steps: 
 A handover prompt is generated, with which a developer can instruct Joule to create an adaptation project in a pro-code IDE, 
 existing key user changes are moved into that adaptation project to be carried forward in that project structure, and 
 Joule supports within the SAPUI5 Adaptation Editor to create developer adaptations based on the given prompt, e.g. by adding custom code, XML fragment or controller extensions. 
 Both capabilities are in active development: Joule enablement for key user adaptation and Developer adaptation: MCP support for fragment & controller extensions . See a preview in Agentic UI Extensibility: The Next Chapter of SAPUI5 Flexibility . 

 Where to Start 
 If you want to experience AI-powered SAPUI5 development firsthand, try the new tutorial " Agentic UI development with SAPUI5 ” , which covers the main aspects in a single session: creating a SAPUI5 app with AI, converting it to TypeScript, and modernizing a legacy app, all using the UI5 Plugins for your coding agents. 
 A quick overview of all entry points: 

 What 
 Where

 AI is not replacing what you know about SAPUI5. It is making that knowledge more productive, whether you are building a new app, modernizing an old one, or adapting a standard application. The tools are open source, the entry barrier is low, and the best way to form an opinion is to try them. 
 We are interested in your feedback via GitHub issues . Let us know what works, what does not, and what you would like to see next.

title: Meet Trace IDs: A Flexible Grouping and Traceability Object in SAP Digital Manufacturing
author: ManoelCosta
text:
If you need to group SFCs together, you already have a few options out of the box, like: SFCs with quantity bigger than one, process lots, packing units, etc. They all serve very specific purposes, but every single one of them come with constraints, like requiring SFCs to be of the same material, same routing, same operation, etc. 
 Also, if you have very detailed or specific traceability requirements, you also have a few options, like Data to Collect at Assembly/Consumption, which will also have some constraints. 
 To offer a more flexible solution to address these constraints, we are introducing Trace IDs. 
 Trace IDs takes a very different and much more flexible approach. There are no built-in constraints on what you trace or assign together, and no shared master data context is required. Trace IDs can address more flexible grouping and tracking requirements, like for example giving a physical part a secondary identifier that follows it across multiple orders as its SFC changes, tracking a part by a high value component assembled, or grouping SFCs freely from any master data constraints. 
 In this blog post, I will talk about two different scenarios and how to implement and use Trace IDs in detail.

title: When Does Automation Become Agentic? Part 1 of a Journey from SAP Build Process Automation to Joule
author: Amit86
text:
SAP’s Joule and agentic offerings are evolving quickly, and with every new capability the same practical question comes up in customer conversations: should this use case be classic workflow automation, or does it need an agent? Getting that choice right shapes cost, risk and effort, so consultants and customers alike need a shared way to think about it. This article is the first in a series where I work through that question hands-on, starting with a prototype built on SAP Build Process Automation and moving toward Joule agents 
 One of the most basic questions I wanted to answer for myself is: 
 How do we determine whether a use case should be designed as classic workflow automation or as an agentic solution powered by Joule? 
 Several SAP articles already explain the differences between classic process automation and Joule skills and agents. Here is what I took away as the key differences: 

 Criteria 
 Deterministic automation (with/without AI) 
 Agentic automation 

 Who decides the path? 
 The designer, in advance 
 The agent, at runtime, within guardrails 

 Role of AI 
 None, or a bounded step (classify, summarise, extract, suggest) 
 Plans, selects tools, evaluates results, decides what to do next 

 Routing 
 Fixed rules and conditions 
 Intermediate findings change the route 

 Inputs 
 Well-defined 
 Often incomplete or ambiguous; may need clarifying questions 

 Outputs 
 Predictable structure 
 Variable: an answer, an action, a recommendation or an escalation 

 Predictability and auditability 
 High: the path is the same every run 
 Lower: needs tracing and evaluation to audit 

 Cost and latency per run 
 Low and stable 
 Higher and variable (multiple calls, tool use, iteration) 

 Best for 
 Known, repeatable, step-based processes 
 Variable, multi-step problems where the next step depends on what was just found 

 Typical SAP building blocks 
 SAP Build Process Automation, optionally with AI Core 
 SAP Joule agents with tool integrations, grounding and observability 
 The simplest test: if you could draw the flowchart before the first run of the use-case, it’s deterministic automation, even with an LLM inside. If the system has to draw it or decide it during the run, it’s agentic. 
 But going beyond the theory, I wanted to explore this question myself from the basics, by building a prototype of a use-case. My goal is to start with a use case that can be achieved with an AI-assisted deterministic process automation and then move to other use cases where conversational Joule capabilities add more value. 
 The use case I selected for the deterministic automation is something familiar to many SAP supply-chain projects: monitoring and analysing SAP queue integration errors (SMQ2) . The very basic version of my use case looks like this: 
 Periodically extract SAP inbound qRFC errors and their corresponding application logs, use an LLM to generate understandable hints to triage and solve the errors and send the result to the relevant team/user. 
 I implemented the core technical flow as follows: 

 Here is a brief description of the various components I used and setup in this workflow: 

 Component 
 Description 

 SAP Build Process Automation 
 Orchestration Platform where we can build the end-to-end automated flow, from extracting S/4HANA errors to invoking AI analysis and handling the results. 

 SAP CAP application (Cloud Application Programming Model) 
 CAP service deployed on BTP Cloud foundry acts as the AI abstraction layer, preparing prompts, calling AI Core, and returning structured queue-resolution hints. 

 SAP AI Core 
 Provides governed access to frontier and open-source AI models used to analyse the queue errors and generate resolution hints. 

 SAP S/4HANA system 
 S/4HANA system containing the operational queue and application-log information being analysed, which can be accessed using oData APIs 

 And below is what the workflow looks like: 

 Step 
 Purpose 
 Technical workflow 

 1. Trigger the workflow periodically 
 Automatically starts the queue-monitoring process at the configured schedule or interval. 
 SAP Build Process Automation (BPA) scheduled trigger 

 2. Extract queue errors and application logs 
 Retrieves failed qRFC queues together with the relevant application-log information from SAP S/4HANA. 
 BPA → BTP Destination → Cloud Connector → OData API → S/4HANA 

 3. Generate AI-based remediation hints 
 Sends the queue error and log context to the CAP service. The CAP service calls the LLM through SAP AI Core and returns an analysis with suggested remediation hints. 
 BPA → CAP application on Cloud Foundry → BTP Destination → SAP AI Core 

 4. Create and store the Excel report 
 Converts the analysis results into a structured Excel report and stores the generated file for further review or distribution. 
 BPA → Desktop Automation → Excel SDK → Write Queue Analysis → Save .xlsx 
 Here are some example remediation hints generated by the above workflow: 
 Invalid SSCC 
 Root cause: Invalid check digit for SSCC 800107140; expected 5. 
 Suggested action: Correct/regenerate the SSCC in the ASN/HU packaging data and reprocess the queue. 
 DLWSXXXCLNT2000180002030 
 Material master issue 
 Root cause: Material XYZ-SOUM-0001 is missing or not extended for plant/warehouse XYZ. 
 Suggested action: Extend the required material and warehouse views, then reprocess the queue. 
 EWMSGM_XYZ007000006762 
 Loading point configuration 
 Root cause: Loading point LP_EWM01 is not assigned to docking location WAREHOUSE-XYZ. 
 Suggested action: Maintain the loading point assignment or correct the inbound data, then reprocess the queue. 
 WMAAXXXCLNT2001236 
 As someone who has assisted users in queue monitoring and resolution, I can appreciate how much time a user can save with the help of the above basic analysis which is generated automatically with periodic monitoring. The final output could also be emailed to the relevant support users via a different workflow in the BPA automation. 
 At this stage, there is AI in the architecture, but there is nothing agentic about it, as the LLM doesn’t choose any tools or actions but responds with a hint. The call to AI Core is made through a lightweight CAP application deployed on Cloud Foundry which calls AI Core to get responses. The benefit of using a CAP application instead of a direct AI Core call via a SAP Build Action is that it gives you a clean abstraction layer which handles AI Core authentication, prompt construction, model calls, error handling, and transforming the LLM response into a predictable structure. The other benefit is reuse and flexibility: the same CAP service can be called from your scheduled BPA process, a Joule skill, a Fiori application, or another integration. You can also change the underlying model, add grounding, or enhance the AI logic later without redesigning the BPA workflow. 
 In Part 2, I’ll move from deterministic automation to an agentic solution built with Joule. I haven’t settled on the use case yet. The test will be the one above: a scenario where the path can’t be drawn in advance and an agent genuinely adds value. I plan to build it with Joule Studio 2.0 once it becomes generally available, and to explore a conversational workflow, document grounding via AI Core, MCP-based integration, and the observability and evaluation capabilities that come with it. 
 This is a learning series, so I’d welcome your feedback and suggestions in the comments. Stay tuned for Part 2!

title: Scheduling BigQuery Jobs Using the Google BigQuery Adapter in SAP Integration Suite
author: YashSonkusare23
text:
Introduction 
 Most integration landscapes have a handful of data preparation tasks that repeat on a clock: filter yesterday's records, remove duplicates, roll up daily metrics, refresh a reporting table. The default instinct is often to build this logic inside SAP Cloud Integration itself, Groovy scripts, Content Modifiers, mapping steps, and move the data through CPI to get there. 
 That works, but it puts SAP CI in a role it isn't built for: a data processing engine. Every record that needs filtering or aggregating must pass through the integration flow's memory and message model, which does not scale well for large tables and adds processing time that has nothing to do with integration logic. 
 There is a simpler split. SAP CI already ships a Google BigQuery adapter that can talk to BigQuery's Jobs resource directly. Instead of pulling data into CPI to transform it, SAP CI can trigger a BigQuery Job on a schedule and let BigQuery do the heavy lifting where the data already lives, then simply monitor the outcome. 
 What Is a BigQuery Job, and Why Trigger It from SAP CI? 
 A BigQuery Job is BigQuery's own unit of asynchronous work: a query, load, extract, or copy operation that BigQuery executes internally and tracks by a Job ID. You don't get results back inline the way you would from a normal API call, you submit the job, BigQuery runs it against its own compute, and you check back on its status. 
 That asynchronous model is exactly why pairing it with SAP CI works well. SAP CI's Google BigQuery adapter can submit a job (an INSERT operation on the Jobs resource) and later poll for its status, without ever having the underlying dataset pass through the integration flow. The data never leaves BigQuery; only the instruction to process it, and the status of that instruction, cross the wire. 

 SAP CI 
 BigQuery Jobs 

 Schedules execution (daily/weekly/monthly) 
 Yes 
 — 

 Triggers the job via the adapter 
 Yes 
 — 

 Monitors job status and handles notifications/errors 
 Yes 
 — 

 Executes the SQL (filter, dedupe, aggregate, transform) 
 — 
 Yes 

 Performs MERGE/UPSERT into target tables 
 — 
 Yes 

 Loads, copies, or exports data 
 — 
 Yes 

 Stores results for reporting/analytics 
 — 
 Yes 

 The Processing Capabilities Behind the Job 
 A single BigQuery Job is really a SQL statement (or a load/export configuration) that can combine several operations in one pass. The common recurring-processing patterns look like this: 
 Filtering and deduplication. The job reads from a staging table and applies WHERE clauses or windowed ROW_NUMBER() logic to drop duplicate or irrelevant rows before anything downstream sees them. 
 Good fit: staging tables that accumulate raw or repeated inserts between runs. 
 Keep in mind: dedup logic needs a clear key (natural key, hash, or load timestamp) or it will silently keep the wrong duplicate. 
 Aggregation and metrics calculation. The job groups and summarizes, daily sales totals, counts, averages, turning row-level detail into the shape a dashboard actually consumes. 
 Good fit: reporting tables that are read far more often than the raw data they're built from. 
 Keep in mind: aggregation windows (daily vs. rolling vs. month-to-date) should be explicit in the SQL, not assumed. 
 MERGE/UPSERT into the target table. Rather than truncating and reloading, the job issues a MERGE statement that updates changed rows and inserts new ones, so the target table stays incremental. 
 Good fit: reporting tables that need same-day, idempotent refreshes. 
 Keep in mind: a poorly scoped MERGE condition can update far more rows than intended, test it against a small partition first. 
 SAP CI's Role: Orchestration, Not Computation 
 SAP CI's job in this pattern is deliberately narrow: 
 A Timer start event fires the iFlow on the configured schedule. 
 The Google BigQuery adapter submits the job (equivalent to a Jobs.insert call) with the SQL or job configuration to run. 
 The iFlow polls job status (Jobs.get) until the job reports success, failure, or timeout. 
 On failure, the iFlow raises a notification (email, Slack, monitoring alert) rather than trying to fix or retry the data logic itself. 
 No payload of business data flows through the integration flow. What flows through is a job reference and a status, which is what keeps this pattern lightweight even as the underlying tables grow into millions of rows. 
 Scheduler 
 Sample Job Configuration 
 Example Scenario 
 Every night, an SAP CI iFlow triggers a BigQuery Job. The job reads from a staging table, removes duplicates, calculates daily sales metrics, and runs a MERGE into a reporting table. SAP CI never touches the sales records themselves, it starts the job, waits for BigQuery to report completion, and alerts the integration team only if the job fails. By morning, the reporting table is ready and dashboards reflect current data, without a single row having passed through CPI's runtime. 
 When Should You Use This Pattern? 
 Recurring batch prep (daily/weekly refreshes, metric rollups): trigger a BigQuery Job on a timer; this is the core use case. 
 Large or growing staging tables: keep the transformation in BigQuery rather than routing volume through SAP CI, where message size and processing time become constraints. 
 Logic that changes often (a metric definition, a new dedup rule): since the logic lives in the job's SQL, it can be updated without touching the iFlow itself. 
 Low-volume, one-off transformations: if the data is small and infrequent, doing it inline in SAP CI may still be simpler than standing up a scheduled job. 
 Final Takeaway 
 The pattern here is a division of labour, not a workaround: SAP CI stays in the role it's actually good at , scheduling, triggering, monitoring, alerting , while BigQuery does what its engine is built for: filtering, deduplicating, aggregating, and merging at scale. The result is less integration complexity, no large datasets moving through CPI's runtime, and recurring data processing that scales with the data rather than with the integration flow.

title: Migrating SOAP and XI Fault Messages from SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite
author: ggalves
text:
When migrating interfaces from SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite, the standard message flow typically transfers without issue. Fault messages, however, require dedicated attention. They define the error-path contract that sender systems rely on, and SAP Cloud Integration does not offer a native equivalent to the fault message role found in SAP Process Orchestration. 
 This blog post provides a structured, step-by-step approach for reproducing fault message behavior in Cloud Integration for both the SOAP and XI sender adapters. It covers how to capture the backend fault within an exception subprocess, import the original fault mapping from the ESR, and return the expected fault envelope to the caller — preserving the same structure, values, and HTTP status the sender has always received.

title: SSO with SPNEGO Authentication in NetWeaver.
author: shalabhkumar
text:
SSO with SPNEGO Authentication in NetWeaver. 
 In this Blog i will cover SSO with SPNEGO Authentication in NetWeaver. 
 What is SPNEGO? 
 SPNEGO (Simple and Protected GSSAPI Negotiation Mechanism) is an authentication protocol used in Single Sign-On (SSO) environments. It allows a client and server to negotiate which security mechanism to use, most commonly Kerberos and sometimes NTLM. 
 Overview of SPNEGO. 
 Seamless Single Sign-On (SSO). 
 No repeated username/password prompts. 
 Secure ticket-based authentication. 
 Integration with Microsoft Active Directory. 
 Team Requirements for Configuration SPNEGO SSO. 
 Microsoft AD Team. 
 Linux Team. 
 Basis Team. 
 What is keytab file? 
 A keytab file stores Kerberos security information that allows a server to authenticate with Active Directory without typing a password. 
 What is ktpass? 
 ktpass is an AD-side command used to create a Kerberos keytab file for a service account/SPN, so applications like SAP can authenticate with Active Directory using Kerberos SSO. 
 Linux Team Steps 
 Verify hostname 
 Verify DNS 
 Verify NTP Synchronization 
 Verify connectivity to domain controllers 
 DNS resolution working correctly 
 Basis Team Steps 
 SAP NetWeaver AS Java 7.x---------------------------I have 7.5 with SP 36 Latest. 
 NWA access and UME access---------------------------Yes it is accessing. 
 HTTPS configured (strongly recommended)-------------I already configured HTTPS. 
 Let’s Start SPENGO Configuration. 
 Active Directory Configuration Steps. (AD Team Steps) 
 Step 1 Service User Create in AD. AD Team need to Create a new service account in DC.
Open Active Directory Users and Computers (run dsa.msc or access it from Server Manager). Navigate to your domain → Users container. Right-click → New → User. 

 Step 2 Set password. On the next screen, enter a strong password and select "Password never expires".
Note: Service account passwords should never expire, as an expired password can stop Kerberos authentication working.
Click next to Finish. 

 Step 3 Enable AES encryption flags Open the account Properties → Account tab in the Account options list, enable both AES flags:
This account supports Kerberos AES 128-bit encryption.
This account supports Kerberos AES 256-bit encryption.
Account expires Never.
Note: Enable AES encryption settings for the service account. 
 Below screenshot Properties of Service user account which is AD Team created.
Click on Delegation Tab to check Do not trust this user for delegation option selected.Click on Member of to check Domain Users members of Service Account. 

 Step 4 Register the Service Principal Name (SPN) (AD Team Steps) Before setting the SPN, run nslookup to find the server's exact hostname and any alias names (CNAMEs). This helps ensure the SPN is configured correctly. 
 Now execute below command on Domain Controller to set SPN with only hostname.
setspn -A HTTP/<host> <service-user> 
 Now execute below command to set SPN with FQDN name.
setspn -a HTTP/<FQDN> <service-user> 
 Checking the SPN status with below command.
setspn -l <service-user> 

 SPN has been set properly. 
 Step 5 Generate the Kerberos keytab file. Below is command syntax.
ktpass -princ HTTP/<fqdn>@DOMAIN.COM -mapuser <ServiceAccount> -crypto AES256-SHA1 -ptype KRB5_NT_PRINCIPAL -pass * -out sap.keytab
Below command need to run in AD Server to generate keytab file. (AD Team Steps)
C:\> ktpass -princ HTTP/prd02807.kr-internal.nat@GEO-INTERNEL.NAT -mapuser SVC-GLEBE-PRD-AD -pass "F-2AJJYA$Wb4BCrN3N#S4" -ptype KRB5_NT_PRINCIPAL -crypto AES256-SHA1 -out prdhost.keytab
Keytab file will create with prdhost.keytab name.Meaning of important parameters
princ → Kerberos principal/SPN, for example HTTP/server.domain.com@DOMAIN.COM
mapuser → AD service account associated with the principal
pass * → prompts for the service-account password
ptype KRB5_NT_PRINCIPAL → specifies the principal type
crypto AES256-SHA1 → generates an AES256 Kerberos key
out → name/path of the generated. keytab file 
 Step 6 Open User Management Page and Click on Configuration. (Basis Team Steps) 

 Click on LDAP Server. 
 Server Name----will be LDAP Server IP.
Server Port----389 is LDAP Port.
Username is----Service AD Account SVC-GLOBE-SID.
Password-------Service Account Password.
Then Validate Configuration If password is correct Connection Test Successful will come. 

 Step 6.1 Now Login on NWA Configuration Authentication and Single Sign-On. 
 Click on SPNEGO Add Manually Next 

 On the Pop-up window provide Realm Name as “Test-ABC” and description DEV.
Click Next
On Principal Name screen provide Principal Name as “Service Username-<SID>-SPNego” where <SID> is system for which we are running wizard and its password.
Click Next 

 SVC-GLOBE-DEV is Service username which is created in AD. 

 Finish. 

 You need to Enable it after Finish. 

 Step 7 You need to import keytab file here which AD Team will provide to you. 

 Press Ok. 

 Step 7 Now click on Authentication Tab 
 Select ticket and below red bracket on right bottom side option should be selected. 

 Step 8 Take SAP Application restart. Take SAP Application restart.
stopsap 
 Now Start Application.
startsap 

 Step 8.1 Monitor the Process 

 Step 9 Now run this URL https://host.FQDN:port/irj/portal it will not ask you Username and password. This URL will open without password.
You can see Top right this URL is opened with my ID because my User ID is created in AD. 

 Step 9.1 Now i will run User Admin URL. I am facing below error because I logged in with my LDAP User which is created in AD and this User ID don’t have Roles to login in User Admin URL. 
 Below SAP Note is Solution of above error message.
3255517 - AS Java NetWeaver Administrator not available - Caller Administrator not authorized.
Now you can check my ID in User Admin.
See my ID is in LDAP Data Source and I can logon in NWA / IRJ / user admin URL without entering password.

 Step 9.2 Now I will show you NWA page. It is login with my LDAP ID.
https://hostname:Port/nwa

Solution of above error message.

 Step 10 I was faced one error message while configuring the SPNEGO. 
 Could not validate SPNEGO token.
[EXCEPTION]
java.lang.Exception: Checksum error.
You can find error messages in default.trc
Solution is 1568553 - [AS Java] SPNego SSO fails with Checksum error 

 Conclusion of SSO SPNEGO Authentication. 
 SSO with SPNEGO provides secure and seamless authentication by allowing users to access SAP applications using their Windows/Active Directory credentials without repeatedly entering a username and password. It improves user experience, strengthens security, and simplifies authentication management.

title: Clean Core Operations in Practice: Why Your Operations Team Belongs at the Design Table

title: Auto-Propose Split Parameter

title: Shift Left for Accessibility and Inclusive Design in Corporate Enterprise
author: IrlaRebelo
text:
Picture this: you open your inbox to an email about a design you shipped a few weeks ago. 
 Not a compliment. A fix request. 
 Your work went through the full process, including stakeholder reviews, sign-offs, complete design specifications and delivered to development exactly as expected. And yet, someone navigating the interface right now doesn't know what to do next. 
 They can't see the UI. Without the visual structure guiding the flow that includes hierarchy, spatial grouping, directional cues, the intended next step is invisible to them. Their screen reader moves through the page searching for context that isn't there programmatically. Actions exist on the page, but they aren't associated to their section heading, so the sequence makes no sense. And the button label? It appears three times across the page, identical each time — "Submit," "Submit," "Submit" — stripped of any surrounding context that would tell a blind user which Submit does what, and why. 
 Everything you designed is playing out in real time. Except for the one part that matters most to completing the task. 
 Now ask yourself: what if this hadn't reached you as an internal fix email? 
 What if it had arrived as a customer ticket? 
 This is the moment accessibility becomes real for most designers. And for far too many teams, it's also when the accessibility conversation finally begins: post-release or during a compliance audit. Fixing things at this stage costs ten times more than designing them right the first time. 
 The accessibility testing market is growing by over 50% in the next decade. And this is not because organizations are getting more inclusive, but because they keep catching problems too late [1]. Most accessibility knowledge still lives inside audit firms and QA teams. Designers and the people making the decisions that directly shape user experience are often left out of the loop entirely. 
 We decided to change that.

title: Can CK11N cost a specific valuation type of a split valuated material?
author: aga_c
text:
Hi all, 
 I'm investigating whether split valuation is the right solution for a manufacturing scenario and would appreciate some guidance before I continue with additional testing. 
 The business process is roughly as follows: 
 We have a semi-finished material A . 
 Material A exists in two qualities: 
 a standard quality material produced through the normal process 
 a lower quality version recovered from production instead of being scrapped 
 The recovered material can be used again, but it first needs to go through an additional rework/reconditioning process. 
 To model this, I tested split valuation for material A: 
 Material A has two valuation types, representing the standard and recovered qualities. 
 Each valuation type has a different cost (standard quality cost is derived from BOM and routing, low quality standard cost was set up in MR21, both child level materials have price control S and in-house production settings) 
 Production orders consume the correct valuation type as expected. 
 The process flow is: 
 Standard material A is used in production of FERT. 
 Part of the material is recovered as a by-product and posted back into inventory with a different valuation type and a lower value. 
 Semi-finished material B consumes the recovered stock of material A and performs the reconditioning process. 
 Material B is then used as an alternative input instead of standard material A in the final manufacturing process. 
 The inventory side works correctly. SAP is able to distinguish between the two valuation types and production orders consume the correct stock. 
 The issue appears during costing. 
 Although material B always consumes the lower value valuation type of material A, the CK11N cost estimate for material B does not appear to use that lower valuation . Instead, it seems to cost material A using the standard valuation cost. 
 As a result: 
 Actual consumption is posted at the lower recovered value. 
 Standard costing for material B remains much higher than expected. 
 When material B is later used in production, significant unfavourable manufacturing variances are generated because material B which is still lower quality ends up being more expensive than standard quality material A. 
 My questions are: 
 Is it possible for CK11N to cost a component using a specific valuation type rather than the default material valuation? 
 Is there a standard Product Costing configuration that supports this scenario? 
 Would mixed costing be a suitable approach here, or is mixed costing intended only for alternative procurement/production versions rather than alternative valuation types of the same material? 
 If split valuation is not the right design, how would you normally model a recovered lower quality material that requires additional processing before being reused without creating new material SKU? 
 Any advice or examples from similar implementations would be greatly appreciated. 
 Thanks.

title: SAP Puts Product-Level Cloud Emissions and Energy Data in Customers’ Hands
author: Matthias Medert
text:
SAP is making the carbon footprint of cloud software visible product by product, customer by customer. 

 As climate disclosure requirements tighten and AI-driven workloads reshape cloud infrastructure, organizations need granular, credible emissions data across their value chains. Cloud software is now a material part of most companies’ IT landscapes, yet the industry default remains spend-based estimation: a single carbon intensity factor applied uniformly, regardless of which product a customer runs, where it is hosted, or how much infrastructure it actually consumes. Spend-based data meets minimum reporting thresholds, but it cannot reveal where emissions concentrate or where reduction levers exist. 
 Calculate your corporate and product carbon footprint at scale with ERP-centric, AI-enabled carbon management 

 Learn how 

 With SAP’s cloud product carbon footprint, customers can see the emissions and energy consumption associated with their use of supported SAP cloud products, calculated from the infrastructure activity that serves them. This moves beyond spend-based averages to help give customers a clearer view of their cloud footprint and where potential opportunities to reduce it exist. 

 A new methodology 

 SAP’s cloud product carbon footprint (PCF) helps provide customers with activity-based emissions and energy data for selected SAP cloud products. 

 The core of the approach is a bottom-up energy model. Every day, SAP calculates the electrical consumption of each physical and virtual server running its cloud products, based on CPU utilization, memory allocation, and the power usage effectiveness (PUE) of each data center. 

 Based on the data foundation in SAP’s corporate Configuration Management Database CCIR, the server-level energy figure is then allocated to specific products and customer tenants through SAP’s infrastructure dependency mapping, a graph-based model that traces which hardware resources serve which customers based on the products and services consumed by them. The result: each customer sees the emissions and energy consumption associated with its use of each SAP cloud product. It’s a product-specific, customer-specific figure, grounded in actual infrastructure activity. 

 The methodology is aligned to the GHG Protocol ICT Sector Guidance. The approach, which uses electricity consumption as the leading allocation metric, has been developed with awareness of how leading cloud infrastructure providers structure their own activity-based methodologies. The full methodology document is publicly available for customers and auditors to review. 

 What this means for customers 

 SAP developed this methodology in close collaboration with customers across industries, including financial services, consumer goods, media, and healthcare, as well as cloud infrastructure experts. Through this validation process, customers consistently highlighted a key limitation of spend-based approaches. While these provide a reporting number, they do not reveal where emissions concentrate or where reduction opportunities exist. Several customers described spend-based data as essentially “blind” when it comes to identifying which products or deployment regions drive their cloud footprint. 

 Activity-based, product-level data helps address that gap. For the first time, it can give customers the ability to identify emissions hotspots and potential reduction levers at the level of individual cloud products and deployment locations. 

 The shift also reflects a broader dynamic in supply chain emissions reporting. When customers report their Scope 3 emissions, their cloud software providers are part of that calculation. SAP is one of its customers’ suppliers, and customers are increasingly asking their suppliers for primary, activity-based data rather than estimates. Building the PCF is SAP providing to its customers the same quality of data it asks of its own suppliers. 

 SAP as customer zero 

 SAP uses the same PCF methodology and data for its own cloud portfolio. The visibility we offer customers is the same visibility we apply internally to measure the sustainability performance of our products and to inform our net-zero journey. 

 What the PCF provides internally is a level of granularity that did not previously exist: emissions and energy data specific to each product, each customer, and each region. The leverage points for reducing a product’s footprint, such as infrastructure efficiency, workload optimization, and deployment choices, can now be identified and prioritized at the product level rather than addressed through broad, portfolio-wide measures. 

 What is available today 

 SAP’s cloud product carbon footprint is accessible now through the Finance & Legal section of SAP for Me for a growing list of cloud products, including SAP S/4HANA Cloud, SAP Integrated Business Planning, SAP HANA Cloud, SAP Datasphere, SAP Analytics Cloud, and SAP Commerce Cloud. The underlying methodology is published, aligned to the GHG Protocol ICT Sector Guidance, and publicly available. The full and up-to-date list of covered products is published in the methodology document, which is updated quarterly. 

 For customers using the activity-based PCF alongside SAP’s existing spend-based carbon intensity factor, the spend-based method continues to be available and remains the reference approach for emissions reporting at this stage. Over time, as the activity-based methodology matures and product coverage expands, SAP’s positioning on this will evolve accordingly. As with any carbon accounting methodology, customers should assess their approach in line with their own reporting frameworks and auditor expectations. 

 Outlook 

 With a published methodology, a growing product portfolio, and data already accessible to customers, the cloud product carbon footprint is an established capability that SAP intends to continue developing. 

 In the coming quarters, SAP plans to expand product coverage across its cloud portfolio. Work toward ISO 14067 alignment and external audit readiness is underway. The roadmap includes more detailed scope breakdowns, higher time-resolution data, and integration-ready formats for customers embedding carbon data into their own reporting and operational workflows. SAP is also actively working to reflect the specific emissions profile of AI workloads within the PCF framework. As customers increasingly adopt AI-powered cloud services, extending coverage to these workloads is a near-term priority. 

 For questions about how product-level emissions data can support sustainability and cloud decisions, customers are welcome to reach out to their local SAP contact. SAP also welcomes dialogue with ecosystem peers working on green software or ICT carbon standards. 

 Cloud transformation is increasingly measured on carbon transparency alongside performance, cost, and security. As a frontrunner in activity-based SaaS carbon footprinting, SAP is committed to building that capability openly and to evolving it together with customers and partners. 

 For questions, contact sustainability@sap.com . 

 Matthias Medert is global head of Sustainability at SAP.

title: A Smooth Ride Through Peak Season with Trek Bikes
author: Jin Oh
text:
For many retailers, peak season arrives with Black Friday, Cyber Monday, and the holiday sales that follow. For Trek Bikes , some of its biggest moments happen in March and April, then in late August through early October, when new products are released weekly. 

 No matter what the calendar says, the challenge is similar. When demand accelerates, businesses need to keep pace. For Trek Bikes, that means speed across all aspects of the customer journey. 

 “During our peak seasons, we need speed,” says Royce Thigpen, head of Applications Development for Trek’s SAP Commerce Cloud platform. “We need to make sure that not only is our website stable, but our website is fast, our checkout process is fast, and our ability to get the products to the website from our downstream systems is also very fast.” 
 Build the foundation for agentic commerce with a market-leading e-commerce solution 

 Learn more 

 Keeping commerce moving when the market speeds up 

 The cycling market moves quickly. New products, technologies, competitors, and customer expectations continue to emerge. Trek serves individual consumers alongside a worldwide network of retailers and distributors, so each launch must work across a complex commercial landscape. 

 SAP Commerce Cloud makes it easier for Trek to support consumer and dealer storefronts on a single, reliable platform. Trek can reuse core product information while tailoring each experience to regional availability and customer needs. Localization and extensibility also help the company serve multiple markets without needing to build a separate commerce platform for every region. 

 With a stable commerce foundation in place, Trek can coordinate and validate the product information, marketing content, pricing, and search details needed for a successful launch. This support becomes especially valuable during busy periods, when Trek can release 10 or more products a month. 

 “Not only do we need to have our bikes performing, we need to have our platform performing as well,” Thigpen says. 

 Shifting readiness into high gear 

 Readiness also depends on how quickly teams can respond when something goes wrong. In the past, a commerce incident at Trek could pass through analysts, developers, business analysts, and quality assurance teams. A relatively straightforward issue could take a week or longer to reach production. Each handoff also pulled engineering time away from other development priorities. 

 Preventive support from SAP now helps surface potential issues earlier. Trek has added its own AI -driven automation to analyze those signals and support remediation. Developers review the proposed changes and remain accountable for what moves into production. 

 The results are substantial. Incident resolution that once took one to two weeks can now be completed within a day. Analysis for new SAP Commerce Cloud releases has moved from weeks to hours, and the development path is at least 10 times faster. 

 The shift also gives developers more room to innovate. Thigpen estimates that teams once spent about 25% of their time fixing bugs, but that share is now closer to 1% with the autonomous support pipeline , leaving more time to work on features that improve the customer experience. 

 A smooth ride on the bike — and online 

 Customers experience those improvements in a very simple way. The site works as expected, search responds quickly, checkout keeps moving, and product updates appear when shoppers and dealers need them. 

 Trek’s experience demonstrates that peak readiness goes beyond adding capacity for a seasonal traffic surge. A commerce foundation that adapts continuously, surfaces issues early, and supports faster decisions helps keep busy periods moving while giving teams more time to improve the shopping experience. The resilience, scale, and performance needed at peak are just as important throughout the year. 

 “One of the things that we pride ourselves on is a smooth ride, whether you’re on the bike or whether you’re on our website. The support we get from SAP Commerce Cloud means every day at Trek is a smooth ride.”
